claim: Median survival of GHRH-KO mice (sexes combined) was increased by 295 days (or 46%) relative to that of control mice (931 days for KO mice vs 636 days for control mice).
source: As shown in Figure 1A, median survival of GHRH-KO mice (sexes combined) was increased by 295 days (or 46%) relative to that of control mice (931 days for KO mice vs 636 days for control mice).
evidence: The claim is supported by survival data presented in Figure 1A and explicitly stated in the text with specific numerical values.

claim: The difference in survival between KO mice and controls was significant based upon a non-parametric test (p<0.001; log-rank test).
source: This difference in survival between KO mice and controls was significant based upon a non-parametric test (p<0.001; log-rank test).
evidence: Statistical significance is reported with specific p-value and test method.

claim: Median survival in female GHRH-KO mice was increased by 290 days (43%; from 666 to 956 days) relative to that of control mice (logrank test, χ2 = 46.7, p<0.0001).
source: Analysis of each sex separately showed that median survival in female GHRH-KO mice was increased by 290 days (43%; from 666 to 956 days) relative to that of control mice (logrank test, χ2 = 46.7, p<0.0001) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sex-specific survival data with statistical analysis.

claim: Male GHRH-KO mice had increased median lifespan by 314 days (from 614 to 928 days) or 51% relative to that of control mice (logrank test, χ2 = 28.4, p<0.0001).
source: Male GHRH-KO mice had increased median lifespan by 314 days (from 614 to 928 days) or 51% relative to that of control mice (logrank test, χ2 = 28.4, p<0.0001) (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by sex-specific survival data with statistical analysis.

claim: GHRH deletion led to a significant increase in maximum lifespan by 33% for females (p<0.05) and by 18% for males (p<0.05) relative to controls.
source: GHRH deletion also led to a significant increase in maximum lifespan by 33% for females (p<0.05) and by 18% for males (p<0.05) relative to controls.
evidence: Maximum lifespan data is provided with statistical significance values.

claim: Both male and female GHRH-KO mice were markedly smaller than normal littermate controls.
source: Both male and female GHRH-KO (KO) mice were markedly smaller than normal littermate controls (Figure 2A).
evidence: Body size differences are stated and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: KO mice weighed the same as control animals at birth.
source: Although KO mice weighed the same as control animals at birth (data not shown), they gained less weight than control mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: Birth weight data is mentioned though not shown.

claim: KO mice gained less weight than control mice.
source: Although KO mice weighed the same as control animals at birth (data not shown), they gained less weight than control mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: Weight gain differences are stated and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Food consumption on a per gram body weight basis was not significantly different between KO and control mice.
source: Food consumption on a per gram body weight basis was not significantly different between KO and control mice.
evidence: Food consumption data is explicitly stated.

claim: Body composition studies showed increased adiposity in both male and female KO mice.
source: However body composition studies showed increased adiposity in both male and female KO mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: Adiposity data is stated and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The KO mice had a significantly decreased RQ compared to their wild-type controls during both the dark and light periods under normal housing conditions.
source: The KO mice had a significantly decreased RQ compared to their wild-type controls during both the dark and light periods under normal housing conditions (Figure 2E), although their oxygen consumption per gram of body weight (measured by VO2) was not different from controls (Figure 2B).
evidence: RQ measurements are stated and shown in Figures 2B and 2E.

claim: Oxygen consumption per gram of body weight (measured by VO2) was not different from controls in KO mice.
source: The KO mice had a significantly decreased RQ compared to their wild-type controls during both the dark and light periods under normal housing conditions (Figure 2E), although their oxygen consumption per gram of body weight (measured by VO2) was not different from controls (Figure 2B).
evidence: VO2 measurements are stated and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: KO mice were significantly more active than their wild-type counterparts on measures of spontaneous home cage activity.
source: Interestingly, on measures of spontaneous home cage activity (Figure 2D), KO mice were significantly more active than their wild-type counterparts.
evidence: Activity measurements are stated and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Plasma glucose concentrations were significantly reduced in both male and female GHRH-KO mice under fasted conditions.
source: Consistent with this observation, plasma glucose concentrations were significantly reduced in both male and female GHRH-KO mice under fasted conditions (Figure 2G).
evidence: Glucose measurements are stated and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The lower score of homeostasis model-assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) indicated that GHRH-KO mice had enhanced insulin sensitivity.
source: Furthermore, the lower score of homeostasis model-assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) indicated that GHRH-KO mice had enhanced insulin sensitivity (Figure 2G).
evidence: HOMA-IR scores are stated and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: IGF-I levels in the circulation were much lower in GHRH-KO mice than controls.
source: As expected from deficiency of pituitary GH, IGF-I levels in the circulation were much lower in GHRH-KO mice than controls.
evidence: IGF-I levels are stated as being lower in KO mice.

claim: Insulin tolerance tests (ITT) showed that plasma glucose concentrations decreased more in KO mice than in control mice.
source: Moreover, insulin tolerance tests (ITT) done in mice fasted for 4 hr showed that plasma glucose concentrations decreased more in KO mice than in control mice (Figure 2H) despite of normal intraperitoneal glucose tolerance tests (IPGTT) results (Figure 2F).
evidence: ITT results are stated and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: GHRH-KO mice had normal intraperitoneal glucose tolerance tests (IPGTT) results.
source: Moreover, insulin tolerance tests (ITT) done in mice fasted for 4 hr showed that plasma glucose concentrations decreased more in KO mice than in control mice (Figure 2H) despite of normal intraperitoneal glucose tolerance tests (IPGTT) results (Figure 2F).
evidence: IPGTT results are stated and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Hepatic levels of phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 and IRS1 were significantly lower in KO mice when compared with controls.
source: Hepatic levels of phosphorylation of these proteins were significantly lower in KO mice when compared with controls.
evidence: Phosphorylation levels are stated as being lower in KO mice.

claim: 141 genes had elevated expression in GHRH-KO mice (FDR < 0.05 and FC > 1.50).
source: Overall, we identified 141 genes with elevated expression in the mutants (FDR < 0.05 and FC > 1.50; Supplementary file 1A), along with 164 genes with decreased expression (FDR < 0.05 and FC < 0.67; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Microarray analysis identified specific numbers of differentially expressed genes.

claim: 164 genes had decreased expression in GHRH-KO mice (FDR < 0.05 and FC < 0.67).
source: Overall, we identified 141 genes with elevated expression in the mutants (FDR < 0.05 and FC > 1.50; Supplementary file 1A), along with 164 genes with decreased expression (FDR < 0.05 and FC < 0.67; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Microarray analysis identified specific numbers of differentially expressed genes.

claim: The most highly increased genes were Sult2a2, Sult1e1 and Spink3 (FC > 38).
source: The most highly increased genes were Sult2a2, Sult1e1 and Spink3 (FC > 38; Supplementary file 1A), while the most strongly decreased genes were Hsd3b5, Slco1a1 and Igf1 (FC <0.02; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Specific genes with highest fold changes are identified from microarray data.

claim: The most strongly decreased genes were Hsd3b5, Slco1a1 and Igf1 (FC <0.02).
source: The most highly increased genes were Sult2a2, Sult1e1 and Spink3 (FC > 38; Supplementary file 1A), while the most strongly decreased genes were Hsd3b5, Slco1a1 and Igf1 (FC <0.02; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Specific genes with lowest fold changes are identified from microarray data.

claim: The 141 increased genes were disproportionately associated with GO BP terms related to differentiation, development and proliferation.
source: The 141 increased genes were disproportionately associated with GO BP terms related to differentiation, development and proliferation, such as positive regulation of mononuclear cell proliferation (GO:0032946), regulation of multicellular organismal development (GO:2000026) and regulation of cell differentiation (GO:0045595) (p<0.01) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis shows enrichment of specific biological processes.

claim: Increased genes were disproportionately associated with KEGG pathways, including 'metabolism of xenobiotics by cytochrome P450' and 'drug metabolism-cytochrome P450' (p<0.04).
source: Increased genes were also disproportionately associated with KEGG pathways, including 'metabolism of xenobiotics by cytochrome P450' and 'drug metabolism-cytochrome P450' (p<0.04).
evidence: KEGG pathway analysis shows enrichment of specific pathways.

claim: Among the 164 decreased genes, there was overrepresentation of genes associated with oxidation-reduction process (GO:0055114), xenobiotic metabolic process (GO:0006805), monocarboxylic acid metabolic process (GO:0032787), and lipid metabolic process (GO:0006629) (p<0.01).
source: Among the 164 decreased genes, there was overrepresentation of genes associated with oxidation-reduction process (GO:0055114), xenobiotic metabolic process (GO:0006805), monocarboxylic acid metabolic process (GO:0032787), and lipid metabolic process (GO:0006629) (p<0.01) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis shows enrichment of specific biological processes.

claim: KEGG pathways overrepresented among decreased genes included 'steroid hormone biosynthesis', 'metabolism of xenobiotics by cytochrome P450' and 'drug metabolism—cytochrome P450'.
source: KEGG pathways overrepresented among decreased genes included 'steroid hormone biosynthesis', 'metabolism of xenobiotics by cytochrome P450' and 'drug metabolism—cytochrome P450'.
evidence: KEGG pathway analysis shows enrichment of specific pathways.

claim: For 11 of 13 CR experiments, the 164 GHRH-KO-decreased genes were biased towards CR-decreased expression, and this trend was significant with respect to 7 of 13 CR experiments (p<0.05 by rank-based GSEA).
source: For 11 of 13 CR experiments, the 164 GHRH-KO-decreased were biased towards CR-decreased expression, and this trend was significant with respect to 7 of 13 CR experiments (p<0.05 by rank-based GSEA; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Gene set enrichment analysis comparing GHRH-KO to CR experiments.

claim: Only 3 of 13 CR experiments showed that the 141 GHRH-KO-increased genes were biased towards CR-increased expression (p<0.05 by GSEA).
source: However, we only identified 3 of 13 CR experiments in which the 141 GHRH-KO-increased were biased towards CR-increased expression (p<0.05 by GSEA).
evidence: Gene set enrichment analysis comparing GHRH-KO to CR experiments.

claim: Cyp2b13 and Igfbp1 were among the genes most strongly elevated in GHRH-KO mice, and expression of both genes was similarly increased in Ames, Snell, Little, Ghr−/− and Fgf21 Tg mice.
source: For instance, Cyp2b13 and Igfbp1 were among the genes most strongly elevated in GHRH- KO mice, and expression of both genes was similarly increased in Ames (mixed background) (Amador-Noguez et al., 2004), Snell (DW/J Pit1dw × C3H/HeJ Pit1dw-J background) (Boylston et al., 2006), Little (Ghrhrlit/lit, B6 background) (Amador-Noguez et al., 2004, 2007), Ghr−/− (B6 background) (Rowland et al., 2005) and Fgf21 Tg mice (B6 background) (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Comparison of gene expression across multiple long-lived mouse models with citations.

claim: Genes most strongly decreased in GHRH-KO mice were also decreased in Ames, Snell, Little, Ghr−/− and Fgf21 Tg mice (e.g., Hsd3b5, Slco1a1, Igf1, Elovl3, Keg1 and Igfals).
source: Conversely, genes most strongly decreased in GHRH-KO mice were also decreased in Ames, Snell, Little, Ghr−/− and Fgf21 Tg mice (e.g., Hsd3b5, Slco1a1, Igf1, Elovl3, Keg1 and Igfals).
evidence: Comparison of gene expression across multiple long-lived mouse models.

claim: Genes altered most strongly in GHRH-KO mice were often similarly altered in mice carrying a liver-specific Keap1-KO mutation.
source: Consistent with activation of Nrf2 signaling in GHRH-KO mice, genes altered most strongly in GHRH-KO mice were often similarly altered in mice carrying a liver-specific Keap1-KO mutation (Yates et al., 2009) (e.g., see Sult1e1, Spink3, Cyp39a1, Hsd3b5, Slco1a1 and Igf1; B6 background; Figure 3B).
evidence: Comparison of gene expression with Keap1-KO mice with citation.

claim: Among the 141 increased genes, the dominant trend was enrichment of hepatocyte nuclear factor (HNF) motifs in upstream regions.
source: Among the 141 increased genes, the dominant trend was enrichment of hepatocyte nuclear factor (HNF) motifs in upstream regions (Figure 3C).
evidence: Motif enrichment analysis of upstream regions.

claim: The strongest enrichment was observed for an HNF recognition site with consensus sequence 5-GTTAAT-ATT-3 (p=7.3e-10).
source: The strongest enrichment was observed for an HNF recognition site with consensus sequence 5-GTTAAT-ATT-3 (p=7.3e-10; Figure 3D).
evidence: Specific motif enrichment with statistical significance.

claim: Among the 164 decreased genes, the strongest trend was increased frequency of a MYC binding site in upstream regions, with consensus sequence 5-CA—TG-3 (p=1.8e-5).
source: Among the 164 decreased genes, enrichment for motifs associated with several DNA-binding proteins was observed (Figure 3C). However, the strongest trend was increased frequency of a MYC binding site in upstream regions, with consensus sequence 5-CA—TG-3 (p=1.8e-5; Figure 3D).
evidence: Specific motif enrichment with statistical significance.

claim: Of 15 phase I mRNAs evaluated, 10 were found to be elevated in liver of KO mice, and seven of these were dramatically elevated compared to controls.
source: Of 15 such phase I mRNAs evaluated, 10 were found to be elevated in liver of KO mice, and seven of these were dramatically elevated compared to controls (Figure 4A).
evidence: RT-PCR analysis of phase I xenobiotic genes.

claim: Most of the hepatic phase II genes were modestly increased in GHRH-KO mice.
source: In contrast, most of the hepatic phase II genes were modestly increased in GHRH-KO mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: RT-PCR analysis of phase II xenobiotic genes.

claim: Sult2a2 was elevated by more than 1000-fold in KO mice.
source: However, Sult2a2, the gene increased most strongly in microarray screening, was shown by RT-PCR to be elevated by more than 1000-fold in KO mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: RT-PCR validation of microarray results.

claim: Expression of phase I and II genes was similar in small intestine of KO and control mice.
source: Surprisingly, expression of phase I and II genes was similar in small intestine of KO and control mice, suggesting that the effect of GH on these genes may be liver-specific.
evidence: RT-PCR analysis in small intestine tissue.

claim: Hepatic expression of xenobiotic genes was robustly elevated in Ames dwarf mice compared to their littermate controls (p<0.01).
source: As shown in Figure 4C, consistent with the pattern in GHRH-KO mice, hepatic expression of these genes was robustly elevated in Ames dwarf mice compared to their littermate controls (p<0.01).
evidence: RT-PCR analysis in Ames dwarf mice.

claim: GH-treatment of Ames dwarf mice dramatically suppressed the elevation of xenobiotic genes including Cyp2b9, Cyp2b10, Cyp4a14, Fmo3 and Sult2a2 (two-tailed t test; p<0.01).
source: GH-treatment of these mutant mice dramatically suppressed the elevation of these genes including Cyp2b9, Cyp2b10, Cyp4a14, Fmo3 and Sult2a2 (two-tailed t test; p<0.01) (Figure 4C), but had no effect on housekeeping control genes.
evidence: RT-PCR analysis after GH treatment with statistical significance.

claim: GH treatment had no effect on housekeeping control genes in Ames dwarf mice.
source: GH-treatment of these mutant mice dramatically suppressed the elevation of these genes including Cyp2b9, Cyp2b10, Cyp4a14, Fmo3 and Sult2a2 (two-tailed t test; p<0.01) (Figure 4C), but had no effect on housekeeping control genes.
evidence: RT-PCR analysis after GH treatment.

claim: There was a profound suppression of IGF-I transcription in the liver of GHRH-KO mice relative to controls.
source: Using real-time RT-PCR analysis, we found a profound suppression of IGF-I transcription and significant up-regulation of Igf2, Igfbp1 and Igfbp2 mRNA levels in the liver of GHRH-KO mice relative to controls (Figure 5A).
evidence: RT-PCR analysis of IGF family genes in liver.

claim: There was significant up-regulation of Igf2, Igfbp1 and Igfbp2 mRNA levels in the liver of GHRH-KO mice relative to controls.
source: Using real-time RT-PCR analysis, we found a profound suppression of IGF-I transcription and significant up-regulation of Igf2, Igfbp1 and Igfbp2 mRNA levels in the liver of GHRH-KO mice relative to controls (Figure 5A).
evidence: RT-PCR analysis of IGF family genes in liver.

claim: Differences in IGF family gene expression were absent in different brain regions, such as cerebral cortex.
source: However, such differences were absent in different brain regions, such as cerebral cortex (Figure 5A).
evidence: RT-PCR analysis of IGF family genes in brain.

claim: GHRH-KO mice were characterized by decreased hepatic phosphorylation of MAPKs, including the MEK, ERK, and P38 kinases.
source: In comparison to littermate controls, GHRH-KO mice were characterized by decreased hepatic phosphorylation of MAPKs, including the MEK, ERK, and P38 kinases, each of which is known to participate in cellular stress responses (Figure 5B).
evidence: Western blot analysis of MAPK phosphorylation in liver.

claim: Brain tissues from GHRH-KO mice showed no change in phosphorylation of MEK, ERK, and P38 kinases.
source: In contrast, brain tissues from GHRH-KO mice showed no change in phosphorylation of these kinases (Figure 5D).
evidence: Western blot analysis of MAPK phosphorylation in brain.

claim: Hepatic IEGs mRNA levels are significantly repressed in GHRH-KO mice.
source: As expected, hepatic IEGs mRNA levels are significantly repressed in GHRH-KO mice (Figure 5C) whereas no alteration was detected in the brains.
evidence: RT-PCR analysis of immediate early genes in liver.

claim: No alteration in IEGs mRNA levels was detected in the brains of GHRH-KO mice.
source: As expected, hepatic IEGs mRNA levels are significantly repressed in GHRH-KO mice (Figure 5C) whereas no alteration was detected in the brains.
evidence: RT-PCR analysis of immediate early genes in brain.

claim: GHRH-KO mice had a higher nuclear level of Nrf2 protein than control animals.
source: As shown in Figure 5E, Western blot analysis of liver lysates showed that GHRH-KO mice had a higher nuclear level of Nrf2 protein than control animals.
evidence: Western blot analysis of nuclear Nrf2 protein.

claim: Each of the Nrf2-dependent genes (GCLM, NQO1, TXNRD, NQO1, metallothioneins 1 and 2) was expressed at higher levels in liver from KO mice than in liver from controls.
source: Each of these Nrf2-dependent genes was expressed at higher levels in liver from KO mice than in liver from controls.
evidence: RT-PCR analysis of Nrf2-dependent genes.

claim: CR produced the expected reduction in body weight in both GHRH-KO and control mice.
source: CR produced the expected reduction in body weight in both GHRH-KO and control mice (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Body weight measurements under CR conditions.

claim: The relative decrease in body weight in response to CR was comparable between KO and control mice in both sexes.
source: The relative decrease in body weight in response to CR was comparable between KO and control mice in both sexes.
evidence: Body weight measurements under CR conditions.

claim: In GHRH-KO mice, CR produced significant increase in overall survival, average, median, and maximal longevity when the data from both sexes were combined (log-rank test, p<0.0001).
source: Kaplan–Meier survival curves (Figure 6A) indicate that in GHRH-KO mice, CR produced significant increase in overall survival, average, median, and maximal longevity when the data from both sexes were combined (log-rank test, p<0.0001).
evidence: Survival analysis with statistical significance.

claim: CR female KO mice out-live AL KO mice by 21% (median lifespan: 1156 days vs 956 days; p=0.0001; logrank test; p<0.0001).
source: Further analysis of each sex separately showed that CR female KO mice out-live AL KO mice by 21% (median lifespan: 1156 days vs 956 days; p=0.0001; logrank test; p<0.0001; Figure 6E).
evidence: Sex-specific survival analysis with statistical significance.

claim: The median lifespan of male CR KO mice does not significantly exceed that of male AL KO mice (945 days vs 928 days).
source: In contrast, the median lifespan of male CR KO mice does not significantly exceed that of male AL KO mice (945 days vs 928 days Figure 6D), but CR still further increased overall survival of male KO mice (logrank test; p=0.0382).
evidence: Sex-specific survival analysis.

claim: CR still further increased overall survival of male KO mice (logrank test; p=0.0382).
source: In contrast, the median lifespan of male CR KO mice does not significantly exceed that of male AL KO mice (945 days vs 928 days Figure 6D), but CR still further increased overall survival of male KO mice (logrank test; p=0.0382).
evidence: Sex-specific survival analysis with statistical significance.

claim: Maximal lifespan of KO mice was increased by CR in both sexes, by 17% for females (p<0.05) and by 9% for males (p<0.05).
source: Applying the method of Wang/Allison, maximal lifespan of KO mice was increased by CR in both sexes, by 17% for females (p<0.05; Figure 6E) and by 9% for males (p<0.05; Figure 6D).
evidence: Maximal lifespan analysis with statistical significance.

claim: Fasting plasma glucose levels were significantly reduced in GHRH-KO AL-fed mice compared with control AL-fed mice (p<0.005).
source: Fasting plasma glucose levels were significantly reduced in GHRH-KO AL-fed mice compared with control AL-fed mice (p<0.005; Figure 7A); CR did not significantly affect the glucose level in either genotype.
evidence: Glucose measurements with statistical significance.

claim: CR did not significantly affect the glucose level in either genotype.
source: Fasting plasma glucose levels were significantly reduced in GHRH-KO AL-fed mice compared with control AL-fed mice (p<0.005; Figure 7A); CR did not significantly affect the glucose level in either genotype.
evidence: Glucose measurements under CR conditions.

claim: Plasma insulin was greatly decreased in N-CR, KO-AL, and KO-CR relative to N-AL.
source: Plasma insulin was greatly decreased in N-CR, KO-AL, and KO-CR relative to N-AL.
evidence: Insulin measurements across different groups.

claim: CR resulted in a significant reduction in plasma IGF-I levels in controls.
source: As expected, CR resulted in a significant reduction in plasma IGF-I levels in controls, whereas IGF-I levels in GHRH-KO mice remained at similar very low levels regardless of their diet (Figure 7A).
evidence: IGF-I measurements under CR conditions.

claim: IGF-I levels in GHRH-KO mice remained at similar very low levels regardless of their diet.
source: As expected, CR resulted in a significant reduction in plasma IGF-I levels in controls, whereas IGF-I levels in GHRH-KO mice remained at similar very low levels regardless of their diet (Figure 7A).
evidence: IGF-I measurements under CR conditions.

claim: The level of adiponectin was higher in GHRH-KO than in the control group (p<0.01).
source: The level of adiponectin, a plasma protein secreted specifically from adipocytes, was higher in GHRH-KO than in the control group (p<0.01; Figure 7A).
evidence: Adiponectin measurements with statistical significance.

claim: CR significantly increased plasma adiponectin levels in both genotypes (p<0.005 and 0.01 respectively).
source: Interestingly, CR significantly increased plasma adiponectin levels in both genotypes (p<0.005 and 0.01 respectively; Figure 7A).
evidence: Adiponectin measurements under CR conditions with statistical significance.

claim: Circulating leptin levels were reduced by CR only in KO mice (p<0.01).
source: Conversely, circulating leptin levels were reduced by CR only in KO mice (p<0.01), while KO AL animals had higher leptin levels than the controls (p<0.05; Figure 7A).
evidence: Leptin measurements under CR conditions with statistical significance.

claim: KO AL animals had higher leptin levels than the controls (p<0.05).
source: Conversely, circulating leptin levels were reduced by CR only in KO mice (p<0.01), while KO AL animals had higher leptin levels than the controls (p<0.05; Figure 7A).
evidence: Leptin measurements with statistical significance.

claim: Fasting plasma triglyceride and cholesterol levels were significantly decreased in KO mice and further suppressed by CR (p<0.05).
source: Moreover, fasting plasma triglyceride and cholesterol levels were significantly decreased in KO mice and further suppressed by CR (p<0.05; Figure 7A).
evidence: Triglyceride and cholesterol measurements with statistical significance.

claim: CR profoundly suppressed serum FGF21 levels in both male and female GHRH-KO and control mice (p<0.001).
source: To our surprise, CR profoundly suppressed serum FGF21 levels in both male and female GHRH-KO and control mice (p<0.001; Figure 7B) whereas isolated GH deficiency had almost no effect on FGF21 levels.
evidence: FGF21 measurements under CR conditions with statistical significance.

claim: Isolated GH deficiency had almost no effect on FGF21 levels.
source: To our surprise, CR profoundly suppressed serum FGF21 levels in both male and female GHRH-KO and control mice (p<0.001; Figure 7B) whereas isolated GH deficiency had almost no effect on FGF21 levels.
evidence: FGF21 measurements in GHRH-KO mice.

claim: The transcriptional levels of FGF21 in the liver were markedly inhibited by CR in both GHRH-KO and control mice.
source: Consistent with plasma levels, the transcriptional levels of FGF21 in the liver were markedly inhibited by CR in both GHRH-KO and control mice (Figure 7C).
evidence: RT-PCR analysis of hepatic FGF21 mRNA under CR conditions.

claim: No change was detected in the levels of the receptor FGF4R and β-Klotho in liver.
source: However, no change was detected in the levels of the receptor FGF4R and β-Klotho in liver (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: RT-PCR analysis of FGF21 receptor components.

claim: Mutations in the insulin/Insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-I) signaling can robustly increase longevity in the nematode C. elegans.
source: For example, mutations in the insulin/Insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-I) signaling can robustly increase longevity in the nematode C. elegans (Kenyon, 2010), whereas in mouse, disruptions in growth hormone (GH) pathway dramatically prolong lifespan (Bartke, 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: In mouse, disruptions in growth hormone (GH) pathway dramatically prolong lifespan.
source: For example, mutations in the insulin/Insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-I) signaling can robustly increase longevity in the nematode C. elegans (Kenyon, 2010), whereas in mouse, disruptions in growth hormone (GH) pathway dramatically prolong lifespan (Bartke, 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Ames and Snell dwarf mice are the most studied mutants in which altered GH signals produce dramatic increases in lifespan.
source: Ames and Snell dwarf mice are the most studied mutants in which altered GH signals produce dramatic increases in lifespan (Brown-Borg et al., 1996; Flurkey et al., 2001).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published work.

claim: A number of aging-related phenotypes are delayed in Ames and Snell dwarf mice, including collagen cross-linking, cataract development, kidney diseases, fatal neoplastic diseases and decline in immune function, locomotor activity, learning and memory.
source: A number of aging-related phenotypes are also delayed in these mice, including collagen cross-linking, cataract development, kidney diseases, fatal neoplastic diseases and decline in immune function, locomotor activity, learning and memory (Bartke, 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Mice with disruption of the GH receptor (Ghr−/−) have markedly increased lifespan with concomitant delay of late life diseases and disabilities.
source: For instance, mice with disruption of the GH receptor (Ghr−/−) have also markedly increased lifespan with concomitant delay of late life diseases and disabilities (Coschigano et al., 2003; List et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published work.

claim: Caloric restriction (CR) has been shown to extend lifespan in many species.
source: Caloric restriction (CR) has been shown to extend lifespan in many species and has been extensively used in experimental gerontology to modulate development of age-related diseases (Weindruch and Sohal, 1997).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: In rodents, CR delays the onset of cancer, atherosclerosis, and diabetes, and typically increases lifespan (by 15% in mice and by 30% in rats).
source: In rodents, CR delays the onset of cancer, atherosclerosis, and diabetes, and typically increases lifespan (by 15% in mice and by 30% in rats) (Swindell, 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: 30% CR confers additional life extension in Ames dwarf mice.
source: For instance, 30% CR confers additional life extension in Ames dwarf mice (Bartke, 2011), but has no additional effect on longevity in male Ghr−/− mice, and only a modest reduction of late-life mortality in Ghr−/− females (Bonkowski et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published work.

claim: 30% CR has no additional effect on longevity in male Ghr−/− mice, and only a modest reduction of late-life mortality in Ghr−/− females.
source: For instance, 30% CR confers additional life extension in Ames dwarf mice (Bartke, 2011), but has no additional effect on longevity in male Ghr−/− mice, and only a modest reduction of late-life mortality in Ghr−/− females (Bonkowski et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: The GHRH gene is required for somatotroph cell proliferation and GH secretion.
source: This gene is required for somatotroph cell proliferation and GH secretion (Alba and Salvatori, 2004).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Decreased ribosomal protein S6 kinase 1 (S6K1) activity has been shown to increase insulin sensitivity.
source: Decreased ribosomal protein S6 kinase 1 (S6K1) activity has been shown to increase insulin sensitivity (Um et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: S6K1 signaling is decreased in the tissues of Ames dwarf mice.
source: Since S6K1 signaling is decreased in the tissues of Ames dwarf mice (Sharp and Bartke, 2005), we speculated that S6K1 signaling may contribute to regulate insulin sensitivity in response to isolated GH deficiency.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Heightened insulin sensitivity is a common characteristic of several types of mice with GH-related mutations and extended longevity.
source: Heightened insulin sensitivity is a common characteristic of several types of mice with GH-related mutations and extended longevity (Bartke, 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: A higher fasting RQ, which indicates lowered fat oxidation, is linked to body weight gain, metabolic inflexibility and insulin resistance.
source: A higher fasting RQ, which indicates lowered fat oxidation, is linked to body weight gain, metabolic inflexibility and insulin resistance (Zurlo et al., 1990).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Recent studies in long-lived C. elegans have linked the up-regulation of xenobiotic pathways with increased longevity.
source: Recent studies in long-lived C. elegans have linked the up-regulation of xenobiotic pathways with increased longevity (McElwee et al., 2004).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Several mouse models of delayed aging are characterized by stress resistance and increased xenobiotic gene expression.
source: This link has been further supported in mammals, given that several mouse models of delayed aging are characterized by stress resistance and increased xenobiotic gene expression (Amador-Noguez et al., 2007; Steinbaugh et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published work.

claim: Overexpression of SKN-1 (Nrf2 ortholog) can prolong C. elegans lifespan.
source: Overexpression of SKN-1 (Nrf2 ortholog) can prolong C. elegans lifespan (Tullet et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Disruption of Keap1, which increases Nrf2 activity, also increases the male Drosophila melanogaster longevity.
source: Disruption of Keap1, which in turn increase Nrf2 activity, also increases the male Drosophila melanogaster longevity (Sykiotis and Bohmann, 2008).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Liver-specific Keap1 knockout mice have increased resistance to hepatic stressor acetaminophen.
source: Intriguingly, as revealed by our microarray comparison, liver-specific Keap1 knockout mice have increased resistance to hepatic stressor acetaminophen and exhibit a very similar hepatic gene expression pattern to the one of GHRH-KO mice (Figure 3A) (Okawa et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work and comparison with own data.

claim: FGF21 plays a major role in eliciting and coordinating the adaptive starvation response and promotes similar physiological changes caused by CR, including decreased glucose levels, increased insulin sensitivity, and improved lipid mobilization.
source: Fibroblast growth factor 21 (FGF21), a critical metabolic regulator of glucose and lipid metabolism, is secreted primarily from the liver in response to prolonged fasting and plays a major role in coordinating adaptive changes such as mobilizing and burning fatty acids among different tissues (Potthoff et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Overexpression of FGF21 markedly extends lifespan in mice.
source: A most recent study has shown that overexpression of FGF21 markedly extends lifespan in mice (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Fgf21 transgenic mice have been found to be acting to suppress GH action.
source: Intriguingly, the Fgf21 transgenic mice have been found to be acting to suppress GH action (Inagaki et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Fgf21 Tg and CR-fed mice show similarity with respect to their hepatic gene expression profiles.
source: Furthermore, Fgf21 Tg and CR-fed mice show similarity with respect to their hepatic gene expression profiles (Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: In previous studies, CR did not induce transcription of hepatic FGF21, nor did CR alter levels of FGF21 in circulation.
source: In previous studies, however, CR did not induce transcription of hepatic FGF21, nor did CR alter levels of FGF21 in circulation (Sharma et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published work.

claim: FGF21 has been shown to cause GH resistance and inhibit hepatic GH signaling through Stat5-dependent manner.
source: Previously, FGF21 has been shown to cause GH resistance and inhibit hepatic GH signaling through Stat5-dependent manner (Inagaki et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Early life GH (but not thyroxine) replacement almost completely restored Ames dwarf lifespan to the level of wild-type littermate controls.
source: In an attempt to overcome this difficulty, we previously found that early life GH (but not thyroxine) replacement almost completely restored Ames dwarf lifespan to the level of wild-type littermate controls (Panici et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: The little mice carrying a naturally occurring missense mutation in the GHRH receptor (Ghrhrlit/lit) have isolated GH deficiency.
source: The little mice carrying a naturally occurring missense mutation in the GHRH receptor (Ghrhrlit/lit) have isolated GH deficiency (Eicher and Beamer, 1976; Godfrey et al., 1993).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published work.

claim: Increased lifespan was reported in the little model, but the longevity phenotype is less substantial and depends on a relatively low fat content of the diet employed.
source: While increased lifespan was also reported in the little model, the longevity phenotype is less substantial and depends on a relatively low fat content of the diet employed (Flurkey et al., 2001).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Studies in Ghr−/− mice indicate that the presence of a significant extension of lifespan in animals lacking GH signals does not depend on genetic background but the magnitude of this effect tends to be reduced in a long-lived strain.
source: Studies in Ghr−/− mice indicate that the presence of a significant extension of lifespan in animals lacking GH signals does not depend on genetic background but the magnitude of this effect tends to be reduced in a long-lived strain (Coschigano et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Improved insulin sensitivity combined with low insulin and glucose levels are characteristics of a series of long-lived mutant mice and mice with long-term CR.
source: Improved insulin sensitivity combined with low insulin and glucose levels are characteristics of a series of long-lived mutant mice and mice with long-term CR (Bartke, 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Phenotypic features characteristic of metabolic syndrome, including hyperinsulinemia, and insulin resistance, are associated with increased risk of various age-related diseases and with reduced life expectancy.
source: On the contrary, opposite phenotypic features characteristic of metabolic syndrome, including hyperinsulinemia, and insulin resistance, are associated with increased risk of various age-related diseases and with reduced life expectancy (Stensvold et al., 2011; Noale et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published work.

claim: Increased resistance to multiple forms of lethal stress has been consistently associated with lifespan extension in long-lived mutant worms, flies and mice.
source: Increased resistance to multiple forms of lethal stress has been consistently associated with lifespan extension in long-lived mutant worms, flies and mice suggested the appealing idea that the longevity seen in these mutants was a consequence of their stress resistance (Miller, 2009).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: The transcription factor Nrf2 plays a central role in regulating many antioxidant-related genes against multiple types of stress.
source: The transcription factor Nrf2 plays a central role in regulating many antioxidant-related genes against multiple types of stress (Ma, 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Under normal conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytosol by Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2.
source: Under normal conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytosol by Keap1, the cytosolic repressor of Nrf2. In response to various stress, Nrf2/Keap1 binding is disrupted, and Nrf2 translocates into the nucleus to stimulate the activation of various antioxidant-associated genes (Ma, 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: In response to various stress, Nrf2/Keap1 binding is disrupted, and Nrf2 translocates into the nucleus to stimulate the activation of various antioxidant-associated genes.
source: In response to various stress, Nrf2/Keap1 binding is disrupted, and Nrf2 translocates into the nucleus to stimulate the activation of various antioxidant-associated genes (Ma, 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: It has been proposed that a generalized up-regulation of xenobiotic detoxification pathways may be a shared feature of long-lived mutants and a key mechanism of longevity assurance.
source: Recently, it has been proposed that a generalized up-regulation of xenobiotic detoxification pathways may be a shared feature of long-lived mutants and a key mechanism of longevity assurance (McElwee et al., 2004; Shore et al., 2012; Steinbaugh et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published work.

claim: Some studies have shown elevation of bile acids (as endogenous xenobiotics) level and altered bile acid metabolism in GH deficient mice.
source: Some studies have shown elevation of bile acids (as endogenous xenobiotics) level and altered bile acid metabolism in GH deficient mice (Amador-Noguez et al., 2004, 2007).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published work.

claim: Several GH-mediated transcriptional factors including Nrf2, STAT 5b, and hepatic nuclear factor (HNF) 4alpha have been shown to play an important role in xenobiotic gene expressions.
source: Moreover, several GH-mediated transcriptional factors including Nrf2, STAT 5b, and hepatic nuclear factor (HNF) 4alpha have been shown to play an important role in xenobiotic gene expressions (Waxman and Holloway, 2009; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published work.

claim: Based upon findings in other GH-related long-lived mutants, reduced incidence and/or delayed onset of cancer may have contributed to extended longevity of GHRH-KO mice.
source: At this point, however, based upon findings in other GH-related long-lived mutants (Ikeno et al., 2003; Vergara et al., 2004; Ikeno et al., 2009), we suspect that reduced incidence and/or delayed onset of cancer may have contributed to extended longevity of GHRH-KO mice.
evidence: Statement is speculative but supported by citations to published work on related models.

claim: Deletion of several genes related to insulin/IGF-I signaling including S6k1 extends longevity only in females.
source: Intriguingly, deletion of several genes related to insulin/IGF-I signaling including S6k1 (Selman et al., 2009), IRS1 (Selman et al., 2008) extends longevity only in females.
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published work.

claim: Deletion of IRS1 extends longevity only in females.
source: Intriguingly, deletion of several genes related to insulin/IGF-I signaling including S6k1 (Selman et al., 2009), IRS1 (Selman et al., 2008) extends longevity only in females.
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Mice with transgenic expression of a GH antagonist do not have increased longevity.
source: Insulin levels are reduced in Ames dwarf, Snell dwarf, and Ghr−/−, but not in transgenic mice expressing a GH antagonist in which longevity is not increased (Coschigano et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Suppression of insulin levels is one of the most consistent and robust responses to CR in mice and in other mammalian species.
source: Suppression of insulin levels is one of the most consistent and robust responses to CR in mice and in other mammalian species.
evidence: Statement reflects established scientific knowledge.

claim: Insulin sensitivity seems to be a common feature found in centenarians.
source: Accordingly, even in humans, insulin sensitivity seems to be a common feature found in centenarians (Paolisso et al., 1996).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: GHRH-KO mice are on a mixed C57BL6 and 129SV background.
source: GHRH-KO mice and their littermate controls (on a mixed C57BL6 and 129SV background) were bred in a closed colony at the RS's laboratory (Alba and Salvatori, 2004), housed under standard conditions (12-hr light/12-hr dark cycling and 20–23°C), and fed Lab Diet Formula 5001 (23% protein, 4.5% fat, 6% fiber) (Nestle Purina, St. Louis, MO).
evidence: Genetic background information provided in methods.

claim: All animals were fed AL for the first ∼12 weeks of life.
source: All animals were fed AL for the first ∼12 weeks of life. Thereafter, the mice were either fed AL (AL groups) or 40% of AL (CR groups).
evidence: Experimental protocol described in methods.

claim: After 12 weeks, mice were either fed AL or 40% of AL (CR groups).
source: All animals were fed AL for the first ∼12 weeks of life. Thereafter, the mice were either fed AL (AL groups) or 40% of AL (CR groups).
evidence: Experimental protocol described in methods.

claim: Microarray analysis was performed on hepatic gene expression in GHRH-KO mice and normal littermates using the Affymetrix Mouse Genome 430 2.0 oligonucleotide array platform (n = 3 per genotype, males, 10 months of age).
source: Hepatic gene expression in GHRH-KO mice and normal littermates was profiled using the Affymetrix Mouse Genome 430 2.0 oligonucleotide array platform (n = 3 per genotype, males, 10 months of age).
evidence: Experimental methods described.

claim: Lower activity of S6K1 in GHRH-KO mice might contribute to the improved insulin sensitivity.
source: Consistent with the evidence in S6k1−/− mice (Selman et al., 2009), these data suggest that lower activity of S6K1 in GHRH-KO mice might contribute to the improved insulin sensitivity.
evidence: Inference based on comparison with S6k1−/− mice and observed phosphorylation data.

claim: Hepatic gene expression patterns in GHRH-KO mice were in partial agreement with those of CR, with stronger concordance among GHRH-KO-decreased genes as compared to GHRH-KO-increased genes.
source: Hepatic gene expression patterns in GHRH-KO mice were therefore in partial agreement with those of CR, with stronger concordance among GHRH-KO-decreased genes as compared to GHRH-KO-increased genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Summary of gene expression comparison analysis.

claim: The effects of GHRH-KO on liver gene expression were correspondent with a feminization of gene expression patterns.
source: We also observed notable trends in which the effects of GHRH-KO on liver gene expression were correspondent with a feminization of gene expression patterns, as well as with the effects of castration in male mice (A/JCr background; Figure 3B) (Rogers et al., 2007).
evidence: Comparison of gene expression patterns with citation.

claim: The effects of GHRH-KO on liver gene expression were correspondent with the effects of castration in male mice.
source: We also observed notable trends in which the effects of GHRH-KO on liver gene expression were correspondent with a feminization of gene expression patterns, as well as with the effects of castration in male mice (A/JCr background; Figure 3B) (Rogers et al., 2007).
evidence: Comparison of gene expression patterns with citation.

claim: Genes increased and decreased in GHRH-KO mice were similarly altered in mice with streptozocin-induced diabetes.
source: Finally, we observed an unexpected trend, in which genes increased and decreased in GHRH-KO mice were similarly altered in mice with streptozocin-induced diabetes (BALB/c background; Figure 3B) (Kobori et al., 2009).
evidence: Comparison of gene expression patterns with citation.

claim: The effect of GH on xenobiotic genes may be liver-specific.
source: Surprisingly, expression of phase I and II genes was similar in small intestine of KO and control mice, suggesting that the effect of GH on these genes may be liver-specific.
evidence: Inference based on tissue-specific gene expression differences.

claim: GH is a direct regulator of xenobiotic mRNAs in hepatocytes.
source: These findings suggest that GH is a direct regulator of xenobiotic mRNAs in hepatocytes and that elevation of such genes in GH deficient mice is a direct consequence of attenuated GH signaling.
evidence: Inference based on GH replacement experiments showing suppression of xenobiotic genes.

claim: Elevation of xenobiotic genes in GH deficient mice is a direct consequence of attenuated GH signaling.
source: These findings suggest that GH is a direct regulator of xenobiotic mRNAs in hepatocytes and that elevation of such genes in GH deficient mice is a direct consequence of attenuated GH signaling.
evidence: Inference based on GH replacement experiments showing suppression of xenobiotic genes.

claim: The local action of GH/IGF-1 within specific tissues underlies heightened stress cellular stress responses in GHRH-KO mice.
source: We hypothesized that the local action of GH/IGF-1 within specific tissues underlies heightened stress cellular stress responses in GHRH-KO mice.
evidence: Hypothesis stated by authors based on tissue-specific differences.

claim: Localized regulation of GH/IGF-1-associated mRNAs in the brain is independent of pituitary-derived GH secretion.
source: This is consistent with previous reports in Ames dwarf mice, indicating that localized regulation of GH/IGF-1-associated mRNAs in the brain is independent of pituitary-derived GH secretion (Sun et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Brain tissues from GHRH-KO mice preserve local GH/IGF-I signaling.
source: These data further support preservation of local GH/IGF-I signaling in brain regions of KO mice.
evidence: Inference based on lack of changes in MAPK phosphorylation in brain.

claim: Nrf2 activity might be elevated in GHRH-KO mice.
source: Our microarray analysis uncovered correspondence between the hepatic gene expression profiles of GHRH-KO mice and mice carrying a liver-specific Keap1-KO mutation, suggesting that Nrf2 activity might be elevated in GHRH-KO mice (Figure 3).
evidence: Inference based on gene expression similarity with Keap1-KO mice.

claim: Up-regulation of Nrf2 signaling occurs in GHRH-KO mice.
source: This further supports up-regulation of Nrf2 signaling in GHRH-KO mice.
evidence: Conclusion based on nuclear Nrf2 protein levels and Nrf2-dependent gene expression.

claim: Disruption of the GHRH gene had effects that were only partly overlapping with those of CR, indicating that isolated GH deficiency and CR may extend lifespan by independent pathways.
source: Our microarray analysis of gene expression indicated that disruption of the GHRH gene had effects that were only partly overlapping with those of CR, indicating that isolated GH deficiency and CR may extend lifespan by independent pathways.
evidence: Inference based on partial overlap in gene expression patterns.

claim: Mechanisms underlying extended longevity in GHRH-KO mutants and CR-fed mice are at least partially distinct.
source: These results, taken together, support the idea that mechanisms underlying extended longevity in GHRH-KO mutants and CR-fed mice are at least partially distinct.
evidence: Inference based on additive effects of CR on GHRH-KO lifespan.

claim: The convergence of average body weights of N-AL and N-CR males after 80 weeks of age almost certainly represents age-related weight loss in N-AL animals and its delay in the N-CR group.
source: The convergence of average body weighs of N-AL and N-CR males after 80 weeks of age almost certainly represents age-related weight loss in N-AL animals and its delay in the N-CR group.
evidence: Interpretation of body weight data over time.

claim: FGF21 is speculated to increase longevity by partially mimicking the effect of CR in liver and potentially other tissues.
source: For these reasons, FGF21 is speculated to increase longevity by partially mimicking the effect of CR in liver and potentially other tissues.
evidence: Speculation based on similarities between FGF21 overexpression and CR effects.

claim: The difference in FGF21 response to CR differs from previous studies, potentially due to differences in mouse strains or the use of short-term CR in earlier work.
source: This result differs from previous studies, potentially due to differences in mouse strains or the use of short-term CR in earlier work.
evidence: Speculation about reasons for discrepancy with prior literature.

claim: The FGF21 longevity effect is likely mediated by the GH signaling.
source: Thus, our results further support the idea that FGF21 longevity effect is likely mediated by the GH signaling.
evidence: Inference based on overlap in gene expression and lack of FGF21 change in GHRH-KO mice.

claim: The regulatory crosstalk between GH signaling and FGF21 action may play a pivotal role in controlling metabolic homeostasis during starvation and chronic dietary restriction.
source: Also, the regulatory crosstalk between GH signaling and FGF21 action may play a pivotal role in controlling metabolic homeostasis during starvation and chronic dietary restriction.
evidence: Speculation based on observed relationships between GH and FGF21.

claim: The remarkable magnitude of the extension of longevity in GHRH-KO mice may be related to the relatively short lifespan of normal animals from this strain.
source: The remarkable magnitude of the extension of longevity in GHRH-KO mice may be related in some ways to the relatively short lifespan of normal animals from this strain, approximately 21 months, as compared to approximately 24 months in normal siblings of Ames dwarfs and approximately 29 months in normal siblings on Ghr−/− mice in our colonies (Brown-Borg et al., 1996; Bartke et al., 2001; Bonkowski et al., 2006).
evidence: Speculation about factors affecting magnitude of lifespan extension with citations.

claim: Differences in the genetic background make it difficult to determine whether absence of GHRH, GH or their receptors have quantitatively similar or differential impacts on longevity.
source: Differences in the genetic background of GHRH-KO mice and Ames dwarf, Snell dwarf, and Ghr−/− mice used in previous studies in different laboratories make it difficult to determine whether absence of GHRH, GH or their receptors have quantitatively similar or differential impacts on longevity.
evidence: Discussion of limitations in comparing across studies.

claim: At least some of the gene expression responses observed in hepatic tissue of GHRH-KO mice can be attributed to enhanced insulin signaling.
source: We suspect that at least some of the gene expression responses observed in hepatic tissue of GHRH-KO mice can be attributed to enhanced insulin signaling.
evidence: Speculation based on improved insulin sensitivity and gene expression patterns.

claim: The activation of xenobiotic metabolism pathway protects the tissues from the damaging effects of endogenous and exogenous molecules and thus contributes to maintaining tissue and metabolic homeostasis during aging.
source: In this study, we postulate that the activation of xenobiotic metabolism pathway, presumably through inhibition of GH signaling and alterations of the corresponding transcriptional factors, protects the tissues from the damaging effects of endogenous and exogenous molecules and thus contributes to maintaining tissue and metabolic homeostasis during aging.
evidence: Hypothesis stated by authors based on observed xenobiotic gene upregulation.

claim: Suppression of insulin levels is an important mechanism of life extension by CR.
source: Relating these differential responses to CR to the impact of these mutations on insulin levels lends support to our hypothesis that suppression of insulin levels is an important mechanism of life extension by CR.
evidence: Hypothesis based on correlation between insulin levels and CR response.

claim: Divergent effects of male and female sex hormones on adiposity, adipose tissue distribution, inflammation, cardiac function and/or neuroprotection renders males less responsive to the beneficial effects of reducing insulin, somatotropic and mTOR signaling by dietary or genetic interventions.
source: Perhaps divergent effects of male and female sex hormones on adiposity, adipose tissue distribution, inflammation, cardiac function and/or neuroprotection renders males less responsive to the beneficial effects of reducing insulin, somatotropic and mTOR signaling by dietary or genetic interventions (Bartke et al., 2013).
evidence: Speculation about mechanisms of sex dimorphism with citation.

claim: GH signaling interacts with CR affecting gene expressions and secretion patterns of adipose tissues.
source: These results suggest that GH signaling interacts with CR affecting gene expressions and secretion patterns of adipose tissues in these animals.
evidence: Inference based on observed changes in leptin and adiponectin with CR.

claim: Nrf2 could play an important role in lifespan extension of GHRH-KO mice.
source: Moreover, nuclear Nrf2 protein and many ARE genes were upregulated in GHRH-KO mice suggesting that Nrf2 could play an important role in lifespan extension of these long-lived mice.
evidence: Speculation based on Nrf2 activation in GHRH-KO mice.

claim: Isolated GH deficiency results in improved insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis.
source: Together, these data indicate that isolated GH deficiency results in improved insulin sensitivity and glucose homeostasis.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple metabolic measurements.

claim: The robust increase in both median and maximal lifespan in GHRH-KO mice is consistent with the notion that inhibition of GH signaling ameliorates age-related disease, potentially slowing the aging process.
source: The robust increase in both median and maximal lifespan in GHRH-KO mice is consistent with the notion that inhibition of GH signaling ameliorates age-related disease, potentially slowing the aging process.
evidence: Interpretation of lifespan data in context of aging theory.

claim: GHRH-KO mice provide a new model that can be used to explore links between GHRH repression, downregulation of the somatotropic axis, and extended longevity.
source: We conclude that GHRH-KO mice feature perturbations in a network of signaling pathways related to stress resistance, metabolic control and inflammation, and therefore provide a new model that can be used to explore links between GHRH repression, downregulation of the somatotropic axis, and extended longevity.
evidence: Conclusion stated in abstract summarizing the overall findings.

claim: GHRH-KO mice feature perturbations in a network of signaling pathways related to stress resistance, metabolic control and inflammation.
source: We conclude that GHRH-KO mice feature perturbations in a network of signaling pathways related to stress resistance, metabolic control and inflammation, and therefore provide a new model that can be used to explore links between GHRH repression, downregulation of the somatotropic axis, and extended longevity.
evidence: Conclusion stated in abstract summarizing the overall findings.

claim: The effects of caloric restriction (CR) and the GHRH mutation are additive, with lifespan of GHRH-KO mutants further increased by CR.
source: While these effects overlap with those of caloric restriction, we show that the effects of caloric restriction (CR) and the GHRH mutation are additive, with lifespan of GHRH-KO mutants further increased by CR.
evidence: Statement in abstract summarizing CR experiment results.

claim: GHRH knockout mice exhibit major shifts in the expression of genes related to xenobiotic detoxification, stress resistance, and insulin signaling.
source: GHRH knockout mice are remarkably long-lived, exhibiting major shifts in the expression of genes related to xenobiotic detoxification, stress resistance, and insulin signaling.
evidence: Statement in abstract summarizing gene expression findings.

claim: GHRH-KO mice have increased adiponectin levels.
source: These mutant mice also have increased adiponectin levels and alterations in glucose homeostasis consistent with the removal of the counter-insulin effects of growth hormone.
evidence: Statement in abstract summarizing metabolic findings.

claim: GHRH-KO mice have alterations in glucose homeostasis consistent with the removal of the counter-insulin effects of growth hormone.
source: These mutant mice also have increased adiponectin levels and alterations in glucose homeostasis consistent with the removal of the counter-insulin effects of growth hormone.
evidence: Statement in abstract summarizing metabolic findings.

claim: The endocrine systems play a central role in lifespan determination.
source: Genetic studies in a variety of organisms have revealed that the endocrine systems play a central role in lifespan determination (Tatar et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published work.

claim: Dampening of the GH pathway is the key contributor to lifespan extension in mice.
source: These findings support the hypothesis that dampening of the GH pathway is the key contributor to lifespan extension in mice.
evidence: Hypothesis stated based on evidence from multiple GH-related mutants.

claim: The associated lack of TSH and prolactin makes Ames and Snell dwarf models less than optimal in conclusively exclude the influence of the lack of these hormones on the delayed aging phenotype.
source: Nevertheless, the associated lack of TSH and prolactin makes these two models less than optimal in conclusively exclude the influence of the lack of these hormones on the delayed aging phenotype.
evidence: Discussion of limitations of Ames and Snell dwarf models.

claim: The molecular basis mediating the effects of CR on the aging process remains incompletely understood.
source: Although this phenomenon was first described over 70 years ago, the molecular basis mediating the effects of CR on the aging process remains incompletely understood.
evidence: Statement about current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Phenotypic characteristics of the long-lived mutant mice with disrupted GH axis overlap with some effects of CR.
source: Intriguingly, phenotypic characteristics of the long-lived mutant mice with disrupted GH axis overlap with some effects of CR, suggesting possible mechanistic connections.
evidence: Statement about similarities between GH mutants and CR.

claim: Shared characteristics between GH mutants and CR include: (a) small body size; (b) reduced blood glucose and increased insulin sensitivity; and (c) reduced or absent levels of various hormones and growth factors, that is, GH, insulin, and IGF-I; (d) delaying and/or suppression of the occurrence of several age-related diseases.
source: Shared characteristics include: (a) small body size; (b) reduced blood glucose and increased insulin sensitivity; and (c) reduced or absent levels of various hormones and growth factors, that is, GH, insulin, and IGF-I; (d) delaying and/or suppression of the occurrence of several age-related diseases.
evidence: List of shared characteristics between GH mutants and CR.

claim: Longevity phenotypes in different mouse models may rely on CR-sensitive pathways to varying degrees.
source: Nevertheless, longevity phenotypes in different mouse models may rely on CR-sensitive pathways to varying degrees.
evidence: Statement about variability in CR response across models.

claim: These findings established the GHRH-KO mice as a novel rodent model for delayed aging.
source: These findings established the GHRH-KO mice as a novel rodent model for delayed aging and implicate CR-independent mechanisms in longevity assurance.
evidence: Conclusion stated in introduction summarizing the significance.

claim: GHRH-KO mice implicate CR-independent mechanisms in longevity assurance.
source: These findings established the GHRH-KO mice as a novel rodent model for delayed aging and implicate CR-independent mechanisms in longevity assurance.
evidence: Inference based on additive effects of CR on GHRH-KO lifespan.
